headline: Cape May Rips: Fluke Picky, Bass Gone Nocturnal, Drum Done for the Year
subhead: The rips are fishable but you've got to work the tide right — and the black drum run is a memory until next May.
body_markdown:
Grade for the Rips this week: C-plus. Fishable, not easy. If you'd asked me in April I'd have told you July fluke at the Rips is close to a sure thing on the right tide — and it still is, mostly — but the last few days it's taken more patience than a lot of guys want to give it. Warm water's the reason, and I'll walk you through why.

Water out at the mouth of Delaware Bay has been sitting in the mid-70s, which is warm enough that it's changed the clock on everything. Striped bass down here have gone almost entirely nocturnal — same pattern you're seeing coastwide right now. Daytime, the bass at the Rips are down deep and lockjawed, holding on the current edges but not committing. Dawn and dusk, and especially after dark with the tide moving, that's when they'll eat. My best window the last week has been the top of the outgoing at first light, working bunker-pattern swimming plugs and 2-ounce bucktails with white or chartreuse Bass Assassins along the edge where the ocean push meets the bay current spilling out past Cape May Point. Nothing gaudy — a few keepers in the mid-20s to low 30s, mixed with plenty of shorts. You have to fish it like a night bite even in daylight hours right now, which means working the structure hard and not expecting a blitz.

Fluke's been the more dependable player, but even that bite has gotten picky. Last two hours of the incoming into the first hour of the outgoing, right over the humps and the sandy patches inside the Rips and along the edge of the Hereford Inlet channel, is still putting fish in the box — mostly 16 to 19 inches with a scattered keeper over 20, on white Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with just enough lift to feel bottom. The bite window's tightened up though. Miss that tide change by 45 minutes and you're marking fish on the machine and getting nothing but taps. Triggerfish are mixed in around the wreck and reef structure off the Cape May Inlet jetties in decent numbers for anyone soaking clam or squid strips on the bottom — not a headline fish but a fun one when the fluke go quiet.

Delaware Bay's the more interesting story right now, and it's one we flagged coming — said the weakfish bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings, and that's exactly what's happening. The back-bay channels and marsh creeks up toward Fortescue and along the edges near Brandywine Shoal are holding weakfish again after a slow stretch, and the warm water pushing through those mud-bottom creeks on the dropping tide is concentrating them along the channel edges. Nothing like a blitz yet — call it a steady numbers game, three or four fish an outing for guys working it right — but it's trending up, not down. Bucktail-and-squid-strip combos or soft plastics on light jigheads, fished slow along the drop-offs where the creek water dumps into the main channel on the last two hours of the outgoing, that's where I'd put my time in the evening.

Now the part I know some of you are going to ask about anyway: the black drum run. It's done. May was the show — that's when the big bay drum push up onto the shoals off Fortescue and the mouth of the Maurice River, and by mid-June they're gone, scattered back out to deeper water. If someone tells you they're marking drum in Delaware Bay in July, they're either mistaken or talking about a stray fish, not a run. I'm not going to sugarcoat that one — if drum's what you're after, mark your calendar for next May and don't waste a trip on it now.

Bluefish haven't shown much locally yet. The blitz action everybody's talking about up around Belmar and Raritan Bay hasn't pushed down this far — those bunker schools are still working the central Jersey beaches. If that bait keeps moving south the way it usually does through late July, we could see some of that blue-fish energy show up off the Wildwood beaches and around Hereford Inlet inside two to three weeks. I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet, but it's worth watching the bait reports moving down the coast.

Looking ahead: we're sliding into a first-quarter neap tomorrow, and that's going to soften the current through the Rips for a few days. Less water movement usually means a wider window on both sides of the tide change instead of one hard 90-minute bite — good news for guys who can't time their trip to the exact minute. I'd expect the fluke bite to actually get a little easier to hit through the neap, since the tide won't be ripping through as violently and the fish won't bunch up quite as tight to structure. Striped bass will stay a low-light game until this water cools off, which isn't happening anytime soon in July. And keep an eye on that weakfish pattern in the bay — if the calm, warm evenings hold, I expect those numbers in the marsh creeks to keep building through the end of the month.
